scope: Corollary 10.1 (Almost-linear f-factor search) of the manuscript “Almost-Linear-Time Maximum-Cardinality Matching in General Graphs” (preprints/Almost-Linear-Time-Maximum-Cardinality-Matching-in-Sparse-General-Graphs-September-24-2026/main.pdf), one of the manuscripts of result family 120 of openai/math at commit 1581d4cbdd69. The statement is quoted verbatim from the text that pdftotext 24.02.0 (-raw -enc UTF-8) extracts from the PDF (SHA-256 3cce6ec72ecade69), with whitespace normalised, and was found there under this heading on PDF page 81. Text extraction flattens typeset mathematics (superscripts, subscripts, fractions, large operators, delimiters), so the quote can read differently from the typeset statement and can carry characters with no Unicode meaning; the PDF is authoritative. Finding the quote shows that the manuscript states it, not that it is true. AMVO has checked nothing about this claim.
statement: There are a single uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm, fixed constants cf ≥ 2 and Cf ≥ 1, and a nonincreasing function ηf : N≥1 → R≥0 with ηf (q) → 0 as q → ∞ such that the following holds. The input is a simple graph G = ([n], E) with n ≥ 1, m = |E|, and p = n + m, in the adjacency-list representation of Section 1, together with one-word integers f(v) satisfying 0 ≤ f(v) ≤ degG(v) for all v. With the instruction set and costs of Section 1 and word length wf = ⌈cf log2(n + 2)⌉, the algorithm halts on every computation path in at most Cf p1+ηf (p) instructions. Every output is either an explicit edge list of a valid f-factor or NO. If an f-factor exists, it returns one with probability at least 2/3; otherwise it always returns NO.
